title: Working tree, staging, commit
learningObjectives: Explain working tree, staging, commit and use browser or version-control tools to diagnose and publish reliable web projects.

understand.concept: Git distinguishes the working tree, staging area (index), and committed history. git add stages selected changes; git commit records the staged snapshot. git status shows which changes are modified, staged, or untracked.
understand.whyItMatters: Staging lets a developer choose a coherent change set rather than committing every file change automatically.
understand.analogy: The working tree is the workbench, staging is the tray of selected work, and commit is the recorded checkpoint.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; actual developer tools, Git behaviour, and deployment requirements depend on the browser, repository, and hosting provider.

explain.narrative: The sequence checks the working tree, stages selected files, reviews the staged diff, and records a commit.

examples.code:
# Typical workflow:
git status
git add public/index.html public/styles.css
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Improve lesson layout"
examples.explanation: The sequence checks the working tree, stages selected files, reviews the staged diff, and records a commit.
examples.expectedOutput: The example illustrates the workflow or developer-tool concept; command examples require a practice repository.

practise.guidedTask: Make two unrelated edits. Stage and commit only one, then inspect status and the staged diff.
practise.independentTask: Apply the workflow to a small static site. Capture the commands or browser evidence, identify risks, and document recovery steps.
hints: Inspect actual files and browser behaviour.
Do not commit secrets or personal data.
Verify provider-specific deployment values before changing DNS.
